findings.paper_title: Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – Second Quarter Review 2026-27 A
findings.headline: Five-year revised capital programme totals £718,184k, £8,357k above the original five-year allocation of £709,827k.
findings.detail: The Appendix 3 table shows the revised five-year total by portfolio. Within the total, Children and Young People is £6,398k higher and Economic Development £5,147k higher, while Housing is £7,404k lower.
findings.matters: Showing the five-year total moving up while in-year spend moves down tells a finance director that the in-year reprofiling is moving spend into later years rather than removing it.
findings.figures: £709,827k original five-year allocation; £718,184k revised five-year total; £8,357k five-year variance; £131,747k 2026/27 Q2 forecast

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – Second Quarter Review 2026-27 A
findings.headline: Non-HRA capital financing requirement rises from £460,688k to £463,062k at Q2.
findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement measures the council's underlying need to borrow for capital purposes. The non-HRA figure rises by £2,374k, while the HRA figure is unchanged at £345,505k.
findings.matters: A rising CFR shows the underlying borrowing need growing, which lenders and finance directors track alongside actual debt.
findings.figures: £460,688k non-HRA CFR at 2026/27 indicator; £463,062k non-HRA CFR at Q2; £345,505k HRA CFR unchanged
findings.quote: The Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) measures the Council’s underlying need to borrow for a capital purpose.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – Second Quarter Review 2026-27 A
findings.headline: External debt at 30 September 2026 was £670.182m, against an authorised limit of £844,000k and an operational boundary of £829,000k.
findings.detail: The report states the debt figure is a single point in time and is not directly comparable to the limits. It also says the Q2 Prudential Indicators have not been breached.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director can see the headroom between actual debt and the approved limits at a set date, which is the basis for judging borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £670.182m actual external debt at 30/09/2026; £844,000k authorised limit; £829,000k operational boundary
findings.quote: The Council’s actual external debt at 30 September 2026 was £670.182m.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – Second Quarter Review 2026-27 A
findings.headline: Depot Review forecast reduced by £2.000m to £1.568m, with the balance slipped to future years to develop project requirements and the delivery programme.
findings.detail: The report says the depot redesign project needs further development of requirements and its delivery programme, so the spend is moved into later years.
findings.matters: A £3.500k approved allocation that is largely moved to later years is a delivery timing signal a finance director would track in their own estates programme.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – Second Quarter Review 2026-27 A
findings.headline: City Regional Sustainable Transport Settlement programme scope reduced by £1.618m, with schemes moved to the next Transport for City Regions funding period.
findings.detail: The programme is externally funded through the North East Mayoral Strategic Authority. The report says its scope has been reduced to keep it deliverable within timescales, and the schemes will be put forward for the next TCR funding period.
findings.matters: A council reducing scope on an externally funded programme to meet delivery timescales is a pattern other councils with grant-funded transport schemes will recognise.
findings.figures: £22,783k approved 2026/27 allocation; £7,810k Q2 revised forecast; (1,618) £k variance

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – Second Quarter Review 2026-27 A
findings.headline: Right to Buy capital receipts (HRA) forecast falls from £7.98m at Q1 to £0.64m at Q2.
findings.detail: The Q2 table shows the Right to Buy capital receipts line for the HRA dropping from the Q1 revised figure to the Q2 figure. The report does not give a reason for the change in this table.
findings.matters: A fall in expected receipts changes how much of the HRA programme must be funded from other sources, including borrowing.
findings.figures: £7.98m Q1 revised; £0.64m Q2 revised
findings.quote: Right to Buy Capital Receipts (HRA) 7.98 0.64

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – Second Quarter Review 2026-27 A
findings.headline: Housing portfolio forecast falls by £7.255m to £28.092m, with HRA delivery under an internal service review and several schemes deferred.
findings.detail: The report says HRA capital delivery is subject to an internal service review while alternative delivery methods are assessed. Several housing schemes have been deferred, including Decent Homes, which has a £2.498m variance.
findings.matters: A deferral tied to a delivery-model review shows how an HRA capital programme can shift while its delivery route is still being decided, which other councils with HRA stock may face.
findings.figures: £59.011m approved 2026/27 allocation; £35.347m Q1 revised; £28.092m Q2 forecast; (7.255) £m portfolio variance; Decent Homes (£2.498m variance)
findings.quote: HRA capital delivery is currently subject to an internal service review.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – Second Quarter Review 2026-27 A
findings.headline: Gateshead's 2026/27 capital programme forecast falls to £131.7m at Q2, a £10.5m reduction from the £142.3m Q1 revised budget, after re-profiling across several projects.
findings.detail: The report says planned investment has been re-profiled to and from future years on several projects. The original budget was £165.7m and the Q1 revised budget £142.3m. Actual spend to 30 September 2026 was £34.7m.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare how much in-year reprofiling a capital programme of this size is absorbing, and how it is spread across portfolios.
findings.figures: £165.7m original budget; £142.3m Q1 revised; £131.7m Q2 forecast; £10.5m reduction; £34.7m actual spend to Q2
findings.quote: This has amounted to an overall reduction of £ 10.5m.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 B
findings.headline: The MTFS assumes the Recovery Grant Guarantee and Recovery Grant Top-Up will cease after 2028/29
findings.detail: The paper states that the Recovery Grant Guarantee and Recovery Grant Top-Up are assumed to end after 2028/29. Section 7.2 says the MTFS reflects anticipated reductions to these grants on the basis that they will be rolled into the Revenue Support Grant after 2028/29.
findings.matters: Ending of a grant that supports core funding is a funding change that affects the medium-term gap and that other councils with recovery grant support would also face.
findings.quote: It is assumed that the Recovery Grant Guarantee and the Recovery Grant Top-Up will cease after 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 B
findings.headline: The emissions trading scheme cost pressure of £2.6m is assumed to start in 2031/32, after DESNZ confirmed expansion to waste incineration would not take place in 2028
findings.detail: The paper says DESNZ confirmed in August 2026 that UK ETS expansion to waste incineration would not take place in 2028 as originally intended. The MTFS now assumes the cost applies from 2031/32, in line with proposed EU implementation dates, and will be kept under review.
findings.matters: A national policy deferral that moves a cost pressure outside the current MTFS window changes the medium-term gap for councils with waste contracts.
findings.figures: £2.6m ETS pressure for waste emissions; assumed from 2031/32
findings.quote: In August 2026, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) confirmed that expansion of the UK ETS to waste incineration would not take place in 2028 as originally intended.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 B
findings.headline: The 2027/28 budget includes £11.560m of additional budget cuts and £3.226m of social care interventions, with further proposals still being developed
findings.detail: The interventions table sets out the planned social care interventions and additional budget cuts for each year of the MTFS. The paper says a fully defined set of proposals for 2027/28 cuts will be developed over the coming months to inform budget setting.
findings.matters: The gap between identified savings and the stated gap shows how much of the plan is still to be defined before the 2027/28 budget is set.
findings.figures: £11.560m additional budget cuts (2027/28); £3.226m social care interventions (2027/28); £9.297m additional budget cuts (2028/29); £12.700m additional budget cuts (2029/30)
findings.quote: Further work on developing a fully defined set of proposals for potential cuts to the budget in 2027/28 will take place over the coming months in order to inform the 2027/28 budget setting.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 B
findings.headline: The 2025 pension fund valuation decreased employer contributions, which the paper describes as favourable to the council's financial position
findings.detail: The paper says the last review, performed in 2025, reduced contributions and had a favourable impact on the overall financial position. The next triennial valuation is due in 2028, and no change in contribution rates is assumed in the MTFS.
findings.matters: Employer pension contribution changes are a significant and largely uncontrollable cost driver, and the direction of the last valuation is relevant to peers with similar schemes.
findings.quote: The last review, performed in 2025, resulted in a decrease in contributions and therefore had a favourable impact on the overall financial position.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 B
findings.headline: Capital financing costs are estimated to rise by £9.8m over the MTFS, or by £11.7m if projects do not slip
findings.detail: The paper attributes the increase to new schemes added to the capital programme each year, with slippage assumed on individual projects. It also assumes an average interest rate for new borrowing of 4.8%.
findings.matters: Revenue costs of prudential borrowing, and how sensitive they are to capital programme slippage, bear directly on the budget gap and on borrowing affordability.
findings.figures: £9.8m increase in capital financing costs (with slippage); £11.7m (without slippage); 4.8% average interest rate for new borrowing
findings.quote: Over the MTFS it is assumed that capital financing costs will increase by £9.8m due to additional schemes added to the programme every year but also assuming slippage of the individual projects.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 B
findings.headline: The minimum general reserve for 2026 is set at £10.3m, against a general reserve balance of £21.5m at 31 March 2026
findings.detail: The reserves policy sets the general reserve minimum at 3% of the net revenue budget. The reserves balance table records the general reserve at £21.5m at 31 March 2026, and earmarked balances include Financial Risk and Resilience at £26.1m and Budget Sustainability at £9.3m.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the general reserve headroom above the 3% floor against the reserves being drawn on to balance the budget.
findings.figures: £10.3m minimum general reserve (2026); £21.5m general reserve at 31 March 2026; £26.1m Financial Risk and Resilience; £9.3m Budget Sustainability
findings.quote: (for 2026 this equates to £10.3m)

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 B
findings.headline: Gateshead plans to use £4.000m of reserves to balance its 2026/27 revenue budget of £346.005m
findings.detail: The paper says the 2026/27 budget was agreed on 26 February 2026 and balanced through planned use of reserves. It describes this as in line with the MTFS approach of using reserves to allow time to identify budget cuts and efficiencies. The MTFS policy aims to balance the budget without relying on the general reserve.
findings.matters: Reserve use to bridge a budget year, before cuts are identified, is a pattern peers and lenders track against the stated goal of balancing without the general reserve.
findings.figures: £346.005m revenue budget 2026/27; £4.000m planned use of reserves
findings.quote: which was balanced through the planned use of £4.000m of reserves

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 B
findings.headline: The five-year budget gap rises to £71.337m if only the Adult Social Care precept is raised, and to £85.884m if neither Council Tax nor the precept is raised
findings.detail: The paper sets out two alternative scenarios against the £47.355m base gap. One applies the maximum 2.00% precept increase only. The other applies no increase to either Council Tax or the precept.
findings.matters: A council's exposure to not raising Council Tax, which accounts for 38% of its general funding, is a direct measure of how dependent its gap closure is on local tax decisions.
findings.figures: £71.337m (precept only, 2.00% annual); £85.884m (no increase); base gap £47.355m; Council Tax accounts for 38% of general funding
findings.quote: These alternative scenarios would therefore result in total estimated budget gaps of £71.337m and £85.884m respectively over the five-year period.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 B
findings.headline: Gateshead's MTFS estimates a £47.355m cumulative budget gap over 2027/28 to 2031/32 without further interventions
findings.detail: The annual gap is £14.786m in 2027/28, £12.487m in 2028/29, £16.011m in 2029/30, £0.096m in 2030/31 and £3.974m in 2031/32. The gap assumes Council Tax and the Adult Social Care precept rise in line with Government assumptions of 2.99% and 2.00%.
findings.matters: The size and phasing of an unfunded gap, and the assumptions behind it, show the scale of savings a council must find over the medium term.
findings.quote: The MTFS estimates that without further interventions, a budget gap of £47.355m would occur over the period 2027/28 to 2031/32:

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 B
findings.headline: Adult Social Care, Children's Social Care and Construction Services are named as the most significant budget challenges, with targeted recovery activity in place
findings.detail: The paper identifies three service areas where budget pressures are most significant. It says targeted financial recovery and budget management activity is in place for each. No figures for these overspends are given in this paper.
findings.matters: Peers facing the same social care and construction pressures can compare which areas Gateshead has flagged and how it is responding.
findings.quote: The most significant budget challenges continue to relate to Adult Social Care, Children's Social Care and Construction Services, where targeted financial recovery and budget management activity is in place.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 B
findings.headline: Gateshead reports a provisional 2025/26 revenue outturn with an overall positive revenue balance of £5.701m
findings.detail: The paper says the 2025/26 outturn, including non-service budgets and financing, delivered the budget for the year. The same paragraph notes that the overall position includes overspends in some services.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare how a year-end surplus of this size was reached alongside service-level overspends.
findings.figures: £5.701m overall positive revenue balance (provisional 2025/26)
findings.quote: results in the delivery of the budget for the year with an overall positive revenue balance of £5.701m

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 A
findings.headline: Gateshead says 37 local authorities needed exceptional financial support to set a legally balanced 2026/27 budget, and that Gateshead is not one of them
findings.detail: The paper notes a growing number of local authorities reporting significant financial issues. It records that 37 needed exceptional financial support for 2026/27 and says that, while Gateshead is not in this position, the challenges should not be underestimated.
findings.matters: The count of councils needing exceptional support is a sector-wide benchmark that finance directors and lenders use to judge local government stress.
findings.figures: 37 local authorities needing exceptional financial support for 2026/27
findings.quote: 37 local authorities needed exceptional financial support to set a legally balanced budget for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 A
findings.headline: Gateshead describes significant uncertainty over grant funding from 2029/30 onwards and over retained business rates and the Collection Fund
findings.detail: The paper lists assumptions still to be clarified before February 2027, including grant funding from 2029/30, retained business rates and associated relief grants, the Collection Fund position in January 2027, and the Council Tax base. The funding figures are described as assumed based on the latest information available.
findings.matters: Grant and business rates assumptions beyond 2028/29 drive the size of the funding gap, so their uncertainty affects how far a council's medium-term position can be relied on.
findings.quote: significant uncertainty remains as to the value of grant funding for 2029/30 onwards

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 A
findings.headline: Gateshead's MTFS assumes Council Tax and Adult Social Care precept rises of 4.99% a year for all five years
findings.detail: The paper says the Government's Spending Review assumption is 2.99% a year for Council Tax and 2.00% a year for the Adult Social Care precept. The MTFS aligns with this combined 4.99% for planning purposes, but the paper says actual increases are decisions for Full Council.
findings.matters: A council's assumed Council Tax and precept increases are the largest controllable income line, and a reader can compare that assumption with their own.
findings.figures: 4.99% a year for all five years; 2.99% Council Tax; 2.00% Adult Social Care precept
findings.quote: the MTFS aligns with this assumption and includes an increase of 4.99% for all five years

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 A
findings.headline: Gateshead reports a positive 2025/26 revenue outturn and a 2026/27 first-quarter forecast on target after management interventions
findings.detail: The paper says the council has a strong track record of delivering revenue outturn within budget and describes the 2025/26 outturn as positive. A Cabinet report of 14 July 2026 is cited as forecasting the 2026/27 outturn to be on target after management interventions at first quarter.
findings.matters: A council that has recovered a forecast pressure through management action within the year is a comparison point for other councils facing the same demand pressures.
findings.quote: the projected revenue outturn for 2026/27 at the first quarter was forecast to be on target after management interventions

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 A
findings.headline: Gateshead commits to a plan to replenish reserves to a sustainable level, with use of reserves to balance the budget conditional on a pipeline of budget cuts
findings.detail: The paper says significant use of reserves can only be justified if permanent savings close the estimated gap without further reliance on reserves, and if there is a plan to replenish reserves to a prudent level. It says any use of reserves to balance the budget would need a planned pipeline of budget cuts and interventions.
findings.matters: The stated conditions for drawing reserves set a test a reader can compare with their own council's reserve policy.
findings.quote: There must be a plan to replenish reserves to a prudent level over the medium term.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 A
findings.headline: Gateshead's earmarked reserves include £26.1m for financial risk and resilience and £9.3m for budget sustainability at 31 March 2026
findings.detail: The paper lists four reserve categories. Financial Risk and Resilience covers insurance, grant clawback, workforce development, commercial risk and budget flexibility. Budget Sustainability supports the timing of savings and includes budgets for Corporate Reviews. The paper says reserves can only be used once and will be replenished under a plan.
findings.matters: Reserves held against specific risks, and the use of reserves to time savings, are the mechanisms a finance director would test when a savings plan slips.
findings.figures: Financial Risk and Resilience £26.1m; Thrive £3.9m; Budget Sustainability £9.3m
findings.quote: Budget Sustainability (£9.3m) – Held to support the timings of achieving significant budget savings and Thrive outcomes.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 A
findings.headline: Gateshead holds a general reserve of £21.5m at 31 March 2026, with a stated minimum of 3% of the net revenue budget
findings.detail: The paper lists the general reserve as a statutory contingency that meets any overspend. Balances at 31 March 2026 are described as subject to external audit. The MTFS principles say the council will not rely on the general reserve to balance its budget over the period.
findings.matters: The size of the general reserve against the minimum floor is a standard test of a council's capacity to absorb an unexpected overspend.
findings.figures: General reserve £21.5m; minimum 3% of net revenue budget; earmarked balances including Financial Risk and Resilience £26.1m, Thrive £3.9m, Budget Sustainability £9.3m
findings.quote: Council General Reserve (£21.5m) – A statutory fund that acts as a contingency and allows the Council to meet any unforeseen costs.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 A
findings.headline: Gateshead's MTFS projects income below expenditure in every year from 2027/28 to 2031/32, with the gap in the paper's table widening to £47.4m
findings.detail: The table shows projected income of £351.2m in 2027/28 against projected expenditure of £366.0m, and income of £384.1m against expenditure of £431.4m in 2031/32. The paper says the gap is closed in part by social care interventions and that the largest pressures fall in the first three years.
findings.matters: Showing the income and expenditure lines side by side lets a reader see whether the pressure comes from income growth or spending growth.
findings.figures: Projected income £351.2m (2027/28) to £384.1m (2031/32); projected expenditure £366.0m (2027/28) to £431.4m (2031/32)

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 A
findings.headline: Gateshead estimates a cumulative funding gap of £47.4m by 2031/32 before interventions, with £32.5m of savings still to be identified after £14.9m of social care interventions
findings.detail: The paper sets out a projected cumulative gap that rises from £14.8m in 2027/28 to £43.3m in 2029/30 before interventions. After £3.2m to £3.3m a year of social care interventions, the remaining gap is £11.6m in 2027/28, peaking at £33.6m in 2029/30 and ending at £32.5m in 2031/32. The paper says the largest pressures fall in the first three years.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, can compare the size of the unidentified savings requirement and its timing against their own medium-term gap.
findings.figures: £47.4m cumulative gap by 2031/32 pre-interventions; £14.9m social care interventions over the period; £32.5m savings to be identified; £11.6m additional interventions required in 2027/28; £9.3m in 2028/29; £12.7m in 2029/30; £1.8m in 2031/32
findings.quote: the Council estimates that it will need to close a cumulative funding gap of £47.4m by 2031/32

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 C
findings.headline: Gateshead's impact assessment says a budget gap in the MTFS means savings must be identified from 2027/28 onwards, with no amount given in this paper.
findings.detail: The assessment states that the budget gap identified in the MTFS means significant savings will need to be identified from 2027/28 onwards. It links the reduction in available resources to a potential long-lasting impact on customer experience. The paper gives no gap or savings figure, and points to later impact assessments once savings decisions are made.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, would want to know that the council has an identified gap and a savings requirement starting in 2027/28, even though the size of either is not stated here.
findings.figures: No amounts stated; savings required from 2027/28 onwards.
findings.quote: the budget gap identified in the MTFS document means that significant savings will need to be identified from 2027/28 onwards

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – Second Quarter Review 2026-27 A

findings.detail: The paper records that additional properties have been added to the programme for 2026/27 under the HRA New Build/Acquisition line. The increase is £1.386m against the Q1 revised budget.
findings.matters: Council housing supply growth funded through the HRA is a capital commitment that finance directors weigh against borrowing capacity and rent income.
findings.figures: £2,442k Q1 revised to £3,828k Q2 forecast; increase £1,386k; original allocation £6,664k
findings.quote: Additional properties added to the programme for 2026/27

findings.headline: Gateshead Energy Company Green Heat Network Fund loan forecast reduces by £0.300m to £2.133m, with the first major connection agreement now secured
findings.detail: The paper attributes the £0.300m slippage to future years. It also records that the first major connection agreement for the Gateshead District Energy Network extension has now been secured.
findings.matters: Council lending to its own energy company is a exposure lenders and finance directors track, and a secured connection agreement is a concrete delivery milestone.
findings.figures: Loan £2,433k Q1 revised to £2,133k Q2 forecast; variance £(300)k; original allocation £4,584k
findings.quote: The first major connection agreement has now been secured.

findings.detail: The paper says additional schemes have been added to the 2026/27 programme of works to utilise external funding that is available. Spend on the scheme rises from £3,288k at Q1 to £6,052k at Q2.
findings.matters: Bringing forward externally funded works to draw down available grant is a practice finance directors can compare against their own unspent grant balances.
findings.figures: £3,288k Q1 revised to £6,052k Q2 forecast; increase £2,764k
findings.quote: Increase relating to additional schemes being added to programme of works for 2026/27 to utilise the external funding available.

findings.detail: The paper attributes the increase to cost rises caused by a delay in an external partner signing off design works. The scheme is covered by a Sports England and PSDS grant.
findings.matters: A grant-funded decarbonisation scheme whose cost rises because of a partner's design sign-off delay illustrates a risk finance officers face on externally dependent projects.

findings.quote: Cost increases due to the delay of an external partner signing off design works

findings.detail: The externally funded programme, provided via the North East Mayoral Strategic Authority, has had its scope reduced to ensure deliverability within timescales. The paper says the schemes will be put forward for the next TCR funding period to allow time for design and construction.
findings.matters: A council choosing to reduce scope on a grant-funded programme to meet deadlines, rather than risk returning funding, is a pattern peers managing regional transport grants will recognise.

findings.detail: The funding table shows Right to Buy receipts for the HRA reduced by £7.34m, while the 'Other (Self-financing, borrowing, revenue)' line falls from £58.60m to £55.12m. The paper does not give a reason for the receipts change.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 B
findings.headline: 2026/27 revenue budget balanced using £4.000m reserves; general reserve now at 3% minimum threshold
findings.detail: Council's 2026/27 budget of £346.005m was balanced through use of £4m from reserves, drawing down the general reserve to £21.5m at the 3% minimum threshold against net revenue budget. Council's MTFS principle states it will 'aim to balance its revenue budget without relying on the use of the general reserve over the period of the MTFS', but this is being breached in year one of the planning period.
findings.matters: Annual use of reserves is not sustainable. If the pattern continues as suggested by the five-year gap projections, reserves will be depleted, undermining financial resilience and limiting flexibility to manage risks.
findings.figures: £4.000m reserves used to balance 2026/27 budget; general reserve balance £21.5m at 31 March 2026; minimum threshold 3% = £10.3m
findings.quote: On 26 February 2026, Council agreed a revenue budget for 2026/27 of £346.005m which was balanced through the planned use of £4.000m of reserves.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 B
findings.headline: Budget gap projections assume maximum permitted council tax increases; without them five-year gap reaches £85.884m
findings.detail: The £47.355m gap assumes council tax and precept increases of 4.99% annually (2.99% core increase plus 2% adult social care precept), at levels that do not trigger a referendum. Council models show that if no increases were applied, the five-year gap would reach £85.884m. This demonstrates heavy reliance on maximum council tax increases to manage the budget, and vulnerability to any decision to constrain increases.
findings.matters: Any political decision to limit council tax increases would force much larger spending cuts. The scale of the sensitivity shows the council is structurally dependent on council tax growth rather than having built a sustainable position.
findings.figures: £47.355m gap with 4.99% annual increases assumed; £85.884m gap with no increase; 2.00% precept only = £71.337m five-year gap
findings.quote: These alternative scenarios would therefore result in total estimated budget gaps of £71.337m and £85.884m respectively over the five-year period.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 B
findings.headline: Five-year budget gap of £47.355m will require detailed save proposals to be developed over coming months
findings.detail: MTFS projects cumulative budget gap of £47.355m over 2027/28–2031/32, with £14.786m in the first year. To address this, council plans £3.226m social care interventions and £11.560m additional budget cuts in 2027/28, but these are not yet fully detailed. Council acknowledges that further work must be undertaken on save proposals in coming months to inform the budget setting process.
findings.matters: A £14.8m gap in year one is substantial. The absence of detailed, deliverable save proposals one year before the budget takes effect creates execution risk and raises questions about whether reserves or further contingency measures will be needed.
findings.figures: £47.355m five-year cumulative gap; £14.786m 2027/28 annual gap; £3.226m social care interventions and £11.560m cuts planned for 2027/28
findings.quote: Further work on developing a fully defined set of proposals for potential cuts to the budget in 2027/28 will take place over the coming months in order to inform the 2027/28 budget setting.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 A
findings.headline: Council Tax modelled at 4.99% annual increase (2.99% standard plus 2.00% Adult Social Care precept), but council notes constraints in lower-income area on further rises
findings.detail: The MTFS assumes 4.99% annual Council Tax increase for all five years (aligned with government Spending Review assumptions). However, council explicitly recognises it operates in an area of 'relatively low income and low wealth' and will 'balance the need for increases against the delivery of the Thrive framework and Council priorities', signalling potential political or social constraints on further CT rises beyond this assumption.
findings.matters: Council Tax is a constrained revenue source in lower-income areas; this statement suggests the council may have limited headroom to raise additional revenue via CT increases if the funding gap proves larger, increasing reliance on service reductions.
findings.figures: 4.99% annual increase (2.99% standard + 2.00% ASC precept); assumption applied all five years 2027/28–2031/32
findings.quote: The Council recognises the impact of increases in Council Tax levels and fees and charges in an area of relatively low income and low wealth and will therefore balance the need for increases against the delivery of the Thrive framework and Council priorities.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 A
findings.headline: Available reserves total approximately £60.8m but explicitly framed as one-off, not sustainable for bridging long-term funding gap
findings.detail: Reserves comprise General Reserve (£21.5m, 3% minimum of net budget), Financial Risk and Resilience (£26.1m), Thrive (£3.9m), and Budget Sustainability (£9.3m). Council explicitly states reserves 'can only be used once' and use to balance budget would require 'a planned pipeline of budget cuts and interventions' in future years; without permanent savings, reserves would lead to a 'cliff-edge' funding gap once depleted.
findings.matters: Shows the council has a buffer of ~£60.8m for short-term pressures but understands this cannot solve the structural problem; signals management has realistic view of reserve limits and is focused on permanent solutions, a prudent stance for creditors.
findings.figures: General Reserve £21.5m; Financial Risk and Resilience £26.1m; Thrive £3.9m; Budget Sustainability £9.3m; minimum threshold 3% of net revenue budget
findings.quote: Reserves can only be used once and are therefore not a sustainable source of financing without placing the Council's financial position at risk. Once reserves are depleted there is a risk of a potential cliff-edge

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 A
findings.headline: Multiple significant financial assumptions remain unresolved until February 2027; further clarity expected after 28 October Autumn Budget
findings.detail: The MTFS depends on clarifications still outstanding: grant funding from 2029/30 onwards, 2026/27 pay award impacts, National Living Wage rates, Job Evaluation financial impact, Collection Fund position, Council Tax base, capital programme agreement, 2026/27 budget delivery, and Council Tax and ASC precept rates. Some will only be known after government's Autumn Budget on 28 October 2026; the paper states MTFS will be reviewed after that date.
findings.matters: Any adverse movement in these unknowns could materially worsen the already-identified funding gap; any favorable movement could ease pressure. This is material uncertainty affecting lenders' risk assessment and peer councils' planning.
findings.figures: Clarifications required by February 2027; Autumn Budget 28 October 2026
findings.quote: There are many assumptions in the MTFS that will need clarification between now and February 2027, in particular

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 A
findings.headline: 37 peer local authorities needed exceptional financial support for 2026/27; Gateshead is not in that category but faces substantial challenges
findings.detail: Nationally, 37 local authorities required exceptional financial support to set a legally balanced budget for 2026/27. Gateshead is not among them, placing it in a relatively stronger position than the most distressed councils, but the paper warns against complacency.
findings.matters: Places Gateshead's position in peer context—better than the most distressed but not without material risk; signals council awareness of peer stress and positioning itself as less distressed, relevant to creditor confidence.
findings.figures: 37 local authorities in exceptional support for 2026/27
findings.quote: 37 local authorities needed exceptional financial support to set a legally balanced budget for 2026/27. Whilst Gateshead is not in this position, the challenges facing the Council should not be underestimated.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 A
findings.headline: Funding pressures concentrated in first three years; annual interventions required of £11.6m, £9.3m and £12.7m in 2027/28–2029/30
findings.detail: The funding gap accelerates steeply in years one through three (£14.8m, then £27.3m cumulative, then £43.3m cumulative), with required annual interventions of £11.6m, £9.3m, and £12.7m respectively. Year four requires no new intervention, then £1.8m in year five, suggesting underlying pressures cluster in the early period.
findings.matters: Concentrating acute savings requirements into years 1–3 tests organizational capacity for rapid transformation and may force larger percentage reductions; this also defines the timeline within which policy or local funding sources could alter the position.
findings.figures: Year 1 £14.8m (interventions £11.6m); Year 2 cumulative £27.3m (annual £9.3m); Year 3 cumulative £43.3m (annual £12.7m); Year 4 annual £0.0m; Year 5 annual £1.8m
findings.quote: The largest financial pressures occur in the first three years of the strategy.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 A
findings.headline: 2025/26 revenue outturn delivered positive result despite financial pressure, continuing council's track record of budget control
findings.detail: The council again delivered a positive revenue outturn in 2025/26 despite facing significant service financial pressure. This is described as 'again a significant achievement', indicating a pattern of consistent budget control over multiple years.
findings.matters: Consistent delivery to budget is a key marker of management capability and reduces lender risk from operational weakness; this track record provides some offset to the structural funding challenges ahead.
findings.figures: 2025/26 outturn positive (specific variance not quantified)
findings.quote: The Council has a strong track record of delivering the revenue outturn within budget. The 2025/26 revenue outturn was positive, which was again a significant achievement given the financial pressure faced by services.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy – 202728 to 203132 A
findings.headline: Council estimates cumulative funding gap of £47.4m by 2031/32 with £32.5m in savings still to identify
findings.detail: The MTFS projects a growing funding gap: £14.8m in 2027/28, rising to £47.4m cumulatively by 2031/32. Social care interventions of £14.9m have been identified to manage demand and cost pressures, but this leaves £32.5m in additional savings across all services that have not yet been identified or agreed.
findings.matters: A structural deficit of this scale requires substantial and sustained reductions in service spending or revenue raising, directly affecting the council's ability to meet service demand and signalling material financial stress to lenders and peer councils.
findings.figures: £47.4m cumulative gap; £14.9m social care interventions identified; £32.5m additional savings required
findings.quote: the Council estimates that it will need to close a cumulative funding gap of £47.4m by 2031/32. The MTFS assumes positive interventions to manage demand and cost pressures in social care totalling £14.9m over the period, leaving savings to be identified of £32.5m

findings.paper_title: RTC - Treasury Annual Report 202526 A
findings.headline: All prudential indicators within limits; audit committee and internal audit raised no issues
findings.detail: None of the approved Prudential Indicators for 2025/26 were breached. All debt maturity structures were maintained within agreed upper and lower limits. Audit and Standards Committee reviewed the report on 14 July 2026 with no issues raised. Internal Audit concluded treasury management control systems operating well and all funds safeguarded.
findings.matters: Good governance and audit clearance provides confidence in financial risk controls and compliance framework
findings.figures: Zero breaches of Prudential Indicators; all maturity buckets within approved limits
findings.quote: None of the approved Prudential Indicators set for 2025/26 were breached in the year.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Treasury Annual Report 202526 A
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increased £10.4m to £764.7m; external borrowing up £4.3m to £670.2m
findings.detail: General Fund CFR increased from £408.805m to £419.206m. Total CFR grew from £754.310m to £764.711m. External borrowing increased net £4.281m to £670.182m as £15.0m new borrowing was taken and £10.719m matured. New borrowing was all HRA.
findings.matters: Shows council faces significant ongoing capital financing demands requiring continued external borrowing
findings.figures: CFR £764.711m (increase £10.401m); external borrowing £670.182m (increase £4.281m); new borrowing £15.000m; maturities £10.719m
findings.quote: The total external borrowing as at 31 March 2026 was £670.182m, which was within the operational borrowing limit of £836.000m. This is a net increase of £4.281m from the opening figure of £665.901m.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Treasury Annual Report 202526 A
findings.headline: Council strategy assumes PWLB rates will fall; if wrong, future refinancing costs could be materially higher
findings.detail: Council deliberately delayed external borrowing to use investment reserves instead, banking on forecast interest rate falls. Council explicitly acknowledges this creates refinancing risk: 'Any short-term savings gained from adopting this approach was weighed against the potential for incurring additional long-term costs by delaying new external borrowing until later years when PWLB long term rates are forecast to be lower.' Internal borrowing stood at £94.529m.
findings.matters: The council is taking strategic interest rate risk; a lender needs to understand this exposure and assess whether the rate forecast is credible
findings.figures: Internal borrowing £94.529m (£57.916m General Fund, £36.613m HRA); investment balances £34.814m (down 26% from £47.092m prior year)
findings.quote: Any short-term savings gained from adopting this approach was weighed against the potential for incurring additional long-term costs by delaying new external borrowing until later years when PWLB long term rates are forecast to be lower.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Treasury Annual Report 202526 A
findings.headline: Council delivered net treasury savings of £2.452m through active financial management
findings.detail: Council achieved £2.718m underspend on borrowing costs through strategic use of internal borrowing, partly offset by £0.266m lower investment income. This performance demonstrates effective treasury cost control and day-to-day management.
findings.matters: Shows the council is managing its treasury actively and controlling borrowing costs effectively despite challenging interest rate environment
findings.figures: £2.452m net savings; £2.718m borrowing cost underspend; £0.266m investment income shortfall
findings.quote: Overall Treasury performance against budget for 2025/26 generated net savings of £2.452m

findings.paper_title: RTC - Annual Report of the Audit and Standards Committee 202526 A
findings.headline: External auditor's anticipated opinion on 2024/25 accounts was subject to resolution of matters in relation to pensions.
findings.detail: The external auditor (Forvis Mazars) anticipated issuing an unqualified opinion on Gateshead's 2024/25 financial statements as of November 2025, but this was conditional on concluding pension-related matters that were then outstanding. The committee annual report does not subsequently report whether these matters were resolved or what the final audit opinion was.
findings.matters: An audit caveat linked to pension matters signals outstanding issues related to a potentially material liability that would concern a lender assessing financial risk.
findings.figures: None provided.
findings.quote: they anticipated issuing an unqualified opinion, without modification, on the financial statements. However, this was subject to the conclusion of matters in relation to pensions.

findings.paper_title: KEY - Local Council Tax Support Scheme 202728 B
findings.headline: Local Council Tax Support caseload among working age residents is declining.
findings.detail: The council reports that the number of LCTS claims is currently reducing with no sudden increases expected. As of August 2026, there were 11,701 working age claimants out of 19,451 total. The council acknowledges this could reverse depending on economic conditions and welfare reforms.
findings.matters: A declining welfare support caseload indicates improving resident circumstances and reduced pressure on the council's support spending, though this depends on economic and policy conditions.
findings.figures: Working age claimants: 11,701; Total claimants: 19,451 (August 2026); trend is currently reducing
findings.quote: The number of claims is currently reducing with no sudden increases.

findings.paper_title: KEY - Local Council Tax Support Scheme 202728 B
findings.headline: Council proposes to increase minimum contribution for working age LCTS claimants from 8.5% to 10%.
findings.detail: The council is consulting on increasing the minimum contribution required from working age residents receiving Local Council Tax Support. The impact assessment rates this as 'short term or limited negative impact' on residents' financial circumstances, potentially affecting an estimated 11,701 working age claimants.
findings.matters: A lender would care because changes to Council Tax support schemes affect residents' ability to pay Council Tax and welfare spending, which influences collection rates and the council's budgetary position.
findings.figures: Proposed change from 8.5% to 10%; 11,701 working age claimants affected (out of 19,451 total as of August 2026)
findings.quote: The consultation relates to changing the minimum contribution from working age residents from 8.5% to 10%

findings.paper_title: KEY - Local Council Tax Support Scheme 202728 A
findings.headline: The working-age element of the scheme collects at 68% versus 96.6% for pensioners, and the council explicitly cannot predict how the proposed changes would affect collection rates.
findings.detail: The £186,000 projected saving assumes collection rates remain constant. However, the council states in Appendix 2 that it cannot predict the certainty of collection impact from an increased minimum. The 28.6 percentage point gap between working-age and pension collection rates indicates the working-age element is volatile and sensitive to scheme design, meaning actual savings could vary materially.
findings.matters: Collection volatility on a scheme affecting 11,701 households introduces risk to the financial forecast; the contingent nature of the saving means budget planners cannot rely on it with confidence.
findings.figures: Working age collection rate 68.0%; pension age collection rate 96.6%; working age estimated loss on collection at 68.0% £0.930m
findings.quote: Note it is not possible to predict with certainty what effect an increased minimum contribution would have on collection performance.

findings.paper_title: KEY - Local Council Tax Support Scheme 202728 A
findings.headline: The council is consulting on increasing the minimum contribution from 8.5% to 10%, with modeling indicating potential savings of £186,000, though collection effects are unpredictable.
findings.detail: The scheme currently costs £26.003m and supports 11,701 working-age claimants at up to 91.5% support. Under the proposal, total cost would fall to £25.731m, yielding a £186,000 saving net of collection losses. The scheme has been substantially unchanged since 2013, with this consultation now proposing the first material change in over a decade.
findings.matters: A council signaling budget management through cost reduction in a major discretionary scheme is relevant to revenue forecasting and spending control, even though the amount is modest relative to the total budget.
findings.figures: Current scheme cost £26.003m; scheme cost at proposed 10% minimum £25.731m; potential reduction in cost £186,000; working age caseload 11,701; current maximum support level 91.5%
findings.quote: Potential reduction in cost (incl. loss on collection) £186,000

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: MTFS 2027-28 to 2031-32 - Overview and Scrutiny Report
findings.headline: Council flags 2026/27 budget execution risk: assumes full delivery with no overspend; any slip worsens MTFS position.
findings.detail: The MTFS includes an explicit assumption that the 2026/27 budget will be delivered in full without over or underspends. The council identifies this as an 'important assumption', noting that any overspend would worsen the forward financial position. This signals that the current year budget carries execution risk and is being monitored closely.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand near-term execution risk; if the council is struggling to deliver the current budget, the multi-year projections become less credible.
findings.figures: 2026/27 net revenue budget £346.0m; assumes no overspend.
findings.quote: The MTFS also assumes that the 2026/27 budget will be delivered in full without over or underspends. This is an important assumption as any overspend would worsen the MTFS position going into 2027/28.

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: MTFS 2027-28 to 2031-32 - Overview and Scrutiny Report
findings.headline: Base case assumes 4.99% annual Council Tax increases; alternative scenario shows gap would reach £50.5m if increases taper to zero.
findings.detail: The MTFS base case assumes Council Tax and Adult Social Care precept increases of 4.99% annually throughout the period. An alternative scenario models tapering increases (declining from 4.99% to 0%), which would raise the pre-intervention gap to £65.4m and the post-intervention gap to £50.5m. This shows high income sensitivity to Council Tax increase decisions.
findings.matters: A lender must understand downside scenarios; if the council cannot or chooses not to apply maximum tax increases, the structural gap increases significantly, requiring deeper cuts or greater reserve use.
findings.figures: Base case: 4.99% annual increases, post-intervention gap £32.5m. Tapering scenario (4.99%→0%): gap £50.5m (55% wider).
findings.quote: The MTFS follows this assumption and includes an increase of 4.99% for all five years.

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: MTFS 2027-28 to 2031-32 - Overview and Scrutiny Report
findings.headline: Council commits to ceasing reserve drawdown from 2027/28 and replenishing reserves at £0.5m annually thereafter.
findings.detail: Cabinet agreed in October 2023 to cease drawing from reserves from 2027/28 onwards, and to rebuild reserves by £0.5m per year in 2027/28, 2028/29 and 2029/30. This pivot from drawdown to rebuild represents an important strategic commitment, contingent on the council delivering the full savings programme to close the structural gap by 2027/28.
findings.matters: This is an ambitious timeline requiring successful delivery of an as-yet-incomplete savings plan; failure to deliver will force the council to miss this target or draw reserves further.
findings.figures: Reserve rebuild £0.5m annually in 2027/28, 2028/29, 2029/30; three-year total £1.5m.
findings.quote: In October 2023, Cabinet agreed to extend the planned use of reserves to 2026/27 and cease the planned use of reserves from 2027/28.

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: MTFS 2027-28 to 2031-32 - Overview and Scrutiny Report
findings.headline: General Fund reserves at £21.504m (6.21% of budget), above 3% minimum but will erode if structural gap is not closed.
findings.detail: As at March 2026 outturn, the General Fund balance was £21.504m (6.21% of the £346m 2026/27 budget). The council's minimum reserve target is 3%, equivalent to £10.3m, meaning the council currently has £11.2m of unallocated reserves above minimum. Continued reserve drawdown will erode this cushion if the structural gap is not closed through savings.
findings.matters: A lender needs the current liquidity position and trajectory; adequate reserves now may become inadequate if drawdown continues.
findings.figures: General Fund £21.504m; 6.21% of £346.0m budget; minimum target 3% (£10.3m); above-minimum cushion £11.2m.
findings.quote: Following changes at outturn, the General Fund balance stands at £21.504m, which is 6.21% of the 2026/27 net revenue budget, maintaining a sufficient level of unearmarked reserves.

findings.paper_title: MTFS 2027-28 to 2031-32 - Overview and Scrutiny Report
findings.headline: Council using £8.5m (2025/26) and £4.0m (2026/27) from Budget Sustainability Reserve to bridge budgets.
findings.detail: The council's strategy, agreed October 2023, deploys £8.5m from reserves in 2025/26 and £4.0m in 2026/27 to support the revenue budget. This £12.5m drawdown reflects the council's current inability to achieve structural balance through income and spending alone, and relies on finite reserves to bridge the gap.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown to balance budget is not sustainable; it signals structural deficit and erodes the council's liquidity cushion.
findings.figures: £8.5m drawn 2025/26; £4.0m drawn 2026/27; total £12.5m deployed.
findings.quote: The agreed strategy was to use £8.5m of the Budget Sustainability Reserve in 2025/26 and £4.0m in 2026/27.

The council explicitly acknowledges that further unidentified savings are required to close the remaining £32.5m gap, indicating the savings plan is not yet complete.
findings.matters: A lender assessing feasibility requires realistic, identified savings plans; incomplete programmes present material execution and timing risk.
findings.figures: Identified interventions £14.9m; remaining gap post-interventions £32.5m.

findings.headline: Council faces £32.5m structural funding gap over MTFS period, concentrated in first three years (£11.6m, £11.9m, £12.7m annually).
findings.detail: The draft MTFS shows a pre-intervention funding gap of £47.4m. Identified social care interventions total £14.9m, leaving a post-intervention gap of £32.5m over five years. The gap is front-loaded: £11.6m in 2027/28, £11.9m in 2028/29, £12.7m in 2029/30, then £0.0m in years 4-5.
findings.matters: A lender must establish whether the council has a credible plan to balance its budget; a gap of this scale signals need for service cuts, borrowing, or reserve drawdown.

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: OSC 2026 Financial Outturn Report - Final
findings.headline: The Budget Sustainability Reserve designed to bridge to planned savings has declined from £17.945m to £9.319m in one year, with further £4.0m draw budgeted for 2026/27.
findings.detail: The Budget Sustainability Reserve, established to provide funding "to allow time for a planned schedule of cuts and efficiencies," fell from £17.945m (31 March 2025) to £9.319m (31 March 2026)—a reduction of £8.626m. The 2025/26 budget drew £8.500m; the council has budgeted a further £4.000m draw for 2026/27. If draw-down levels continue at this pace, the reserve will be substantially depleted within approximately two years. This signals either that planned cuts and efficiencies are not being achieved at the assumed rate, or that the reserve was never adequately sized to bridge the structural gap.
findings.matters: This reserve is explicitly temporary—a bridge to allow time for sustainable savings. Its rapid depletion indicates structural cuts or revenue generation is falling behind plan. Once depleted, the council will need to cut services further, generate additional revenue, or rely on other reserve sources, directly affecting operational sustainability and debt-service capacity.
findings.figures: Balance 31 March 2025 £17.945m, 31 March 2026 £9.319m, movement -£8.626m, budgeted 2026/27 draw £4.000m
findings.quote: The budget included £8.500m of Council financing from the Budget Sustainability Reserve to allow time for a planned schedule of cuts and efficiencies.

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: OSC 2026 Financial Outturn Report - Final
findings.headline: The reported positive outturn of £8.401m includes a £6.740m one-off airport dividend; the underlying operational position is significantly weaker.
findings.detail: The council reported a revenue surplus of £8.401m for 2025/26, but this included a £6.740m one-off dividend from Newcastle International Airport shareholding plus other one-off provision adjustments and unbudgeted grant income. The council explicitly states the position "continues to mask significant underlying budget pressures in a number of demand-led services" which "will continue to require close management" into 2026/27. Stripping out the one-off dividend, the sustainable underlying operational position was approximately £1.66m or weaker.
findings.matters: Lenders must distinguish sustainable from unsustainable revenue positions. One-off items do not repeat; if they are masking a structural deficit, the council may lack capacity to service debt in future years without further reserve draws or service cuts. The council's own language signals awareness of underlying pressure.
findings.figures: Outturn surplus £8.401m (including £6.740m one-off airport dividend), Children's Social Care overspend £5.053m, Adults overspend £1.437m
findings.quote: Although the overall outturn was positive, the position continues to mask significant underlying budget pressures in a number of demand-led services. The final position was also affected by several one-off items, including provision adjustments, unbudgeted grant income and the one-off airport dividend.

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: OSC 2026 Financial Outturn Report - Final
findings.headline: Adult and Children's social care overspent by a combined £6.490m in 2025/26 despite receiving £10.187m in additional budget provision for 2026/27.
findings.detail: Children's Social Care overspent by £5.053m and Integrated Adults Services by £1.437m in 2025/26. For 2026/27, the council approved additional budget of £5.535m for Adults and £4.652m for Children. Adult Social Care is explicitly identified as experiencing "significant financial pressure" driven by demand-led costs including high-cost complex placements. Both services have strategic recovery plans (emphasizing early intervention, alternative placements, technology), but continued overspends despite budget increases suggest demand is outpacing the council's ability to control costs through traditional budget management.
findings.matters: Consistent overspends in core, expanding services despite budget allocation increases is a warning that demand may be outpacing control. This threatens future debt serviceability if the pattern continues or worsens.
findings.figures: Adults overspend £1.437m (budget £112.542m), Children's overspend £5.053m (budget £64.431m), Adults additional provision 2026/27 £5.535m, Children's £4.652m
findings.quote: As is recognised nationally, Adult Social Care remains under significant financial pressure, primarily due to demand-led pressures across care packages, including a small number of high-cost transitions arrangement for young people with complex needs moving from Children's Services into adulthood.

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: OSC 2026 Financial Outturn Report - Final
findings.headline: The council holds a £3.792m Dedicated Schools Grant deficit separately; it becomes a General Fund liability on 31 March 2028 when the statutory override expires.
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant overspent by £3.176m in 2025/26, bringing the cumulative deficit to £3.792m as at 31 March 2026. Currently held outside the General Fund under a statutory accounting override (which defers the charge), this override expires 31 March 2028. Unless the DSG recovers or the override is extended by central government, this £3.792m will become a direct charge against the General Fund, further depleting reserves or requiring additional cuts. This is a known, fixed-date liability less than two years away.
findings.matters: Lenders must account for known future liabilities. This represents either an unfunded future charge or a contingent liability that will reduce fiscal flexibility and debt-service capacity unless the deficit is closed or central government extends the override.
findings.figures: £3.792m cumulative deficit, £3.176m 2025/26 overspend, override expiry 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) outturn position for 2025/26 was an overspend of £3.176m, primarily within the High Needs Block. As a result, the cumulative DSG deficit increased to £3.792m at 31 March 2026. In line with the current statutory override, the deficit balance on the DSG is held separately and is not charged to the Council's General Fund. The statutory override is due to end on 31 March 2028.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – First Quarter Review 2026-27 - A
findings.headline: Council's housing development plans revised downward by £4.222m
findings.detail: New build and acquisition schemes have been reprofiled downward by £4.222m to reflect a revised housing growth programme, suggesting the council has reduced its planned housing development output.
findings.matters: Reductions to housing development plans can indicate demand softness or financial constraints. Changes to growth investment plans are material to understanding a council's future position.
findings.figures: £4.222m slippage on new build and acquisitions
findings.quote: Slippage of £4.222m on new build / acquisitions due to reprofiling of schemes to reflect revised housing growth programme.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – First Quarter Review 2026-27 - A
findings.headline: Gateshead Flyover project requires £12.289m additional funding due to work complexity
findings.detail: The major flyover demolition project's budget has increased from £11.725m to £24.014m — an increase of £12.289m. The council attributes this to project complexity and slippage from 2025/26, with completion still expected in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Significant cost overruns on major projects signal delivery challenges and require additional borrowing, indicating capital cost control issues.
findings.figures: Original £11.725m, revised £24.014m, additional funding £12.289m
findings.quote: The flyover is progressing well but due to the complexity of the works involved there was slippage in delivery from 2025/26 and it is expected to be completed during 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – First Quarter Review 2026-27 - A
findings.headline: HRA capital delivery under internal service review with major programme deferrals
findings.detail: The council has initiated a service review of HRA (Housing Revenue Account) capital delivery and is deferring major housing schemes whilst assessing alternative delivery methods. Decent Homes has been cut by £8.978m and demolition/regeneration spend deferred by £9.635m, contributing to a total HRA capital reduction of £23.4m in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A council's ability to execute its capital programme as planned is fundamental to lender confidence. An active service review of housing delivery indicates operational uncertainty in a major capital spending area.
findings.figures: £23.454m HRA variance, £8.978m Decent Homes reduction, £9.635m demolition deferral
findings.quote: HRA capital delivery is currently subject to an internal service review. While alternative delivery methods are being assessed several housing schemes have been deferred, including Decent Homes (£8.978m variance). £9.635m of the variance relates to demolition spend that has been deferred into the following year.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – Year End Outturn 2025-26 - A
findings.headline: Multiple capital schemes dependent on grant funding agreement with North East Mayoral Strategic Authority, creating delivery risk
findings.detail: Two major schemes—Gateshead Quays (£2.0m underspend) and Old Town Hall Quarter (£457k underspend)—were delayed specifically because the council was waiting for grant funding agreements to be finalised with the Mayoral Authority. This external dependency has added uncertainty to delivery timelines.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility on whether capital programmes are under the council's control or dependent on third-party decision-making. Reliance on Mayoral Authority approvals for major schemes introduces governance risk beyond the council's direct management.
findings.figures: Gateshead Quays £2.0m variance, Old Town Hall Quarter £457k variance
findings.quote: Complex scheme resulting in additional time to finalise the grant funding agreement with the North East Mayoral Strategic Authority.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – Year End Outturn 2025-26 - A

findings.detail: A scheme to extend the Gateshead District Energy Network to the Old Fold/Nest estate, originally budgeted at £8.7m, was paused with only £616k spent. The council explicitly states the reason as 'viability issues', indicating the project economics or customer commitment did not stack up.
findings.matters: A lender funding energy transition or infrastructure work needs to understand why schemes fail viability tests. A £8.7m project paused mid-year suggests the council either miscalculated the business case or market conditions changed materially.
findings.figures: £8.669m original budget, £616k outturn, project paused
findings.quote: Project paused due to viability issues

findings.matters: The HRA's asset management and maintenance strategy depends on reliable capital delivery. Scope uncertainty on this scale indicates planning or delivery challenges that could affect longer-term housing condition and viability.

findings.quote: The delivery and scope of works is currently under review.

findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether major infrastructure commitments are progressing on schedule, and persistent delays suggest either project management issues or unforeseen technical complexity that could affect the council's strategic capital plans and delivery capability.

findings.paper_title: TM Annual Report 25-26 Audit & Standards Committee
findings.headline: General Fund Capital Financing Requirement increased by £10.401m to £419.206m, signalling expanding capital commitments
findings.detail: The underlying need to borrow for capital spending grew significantly in one year, reflecting ongoing capital expenditure commitments. Total council CFR reached £764.711m, up from £754.310m. No breakdown is given of the capital projects driving this growth.
findings.matters: Growing capital commitments drive future external borrowing needs. Combined with the current internal borrowing position, this creates timing pressure for refinancing when investment balances run lower.
findings.quote: The Council's underlying need to borrow for capital expenditure and long-term liabilities is termed the Capital Financing Requirement (CFR).

findings.paper_title: TM Annual Report 25-26 Audit & Standards Committee
findings.headline: Council using £94.529m of internal borrowing to defer external borrowing, creating unspecified refinancing risk
findings.detail: The council deliberately used investment balances to fund capital spending rather than borrowing externally, saving on immediate costs but deferring refinancing of this internal borrowing to a future date when rates are expected to be lower. The document does not specify when this refinancing is planned or at what cost.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the refinancing timeline and cost for this significant liquidity commitment, as it represents a future borrowing need that could be substantial if capital programmes accelerate or investment balances tighten.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing £94.529m at 31 March 2026 (General Fund £57.916m, HRA £36.613m)
findings.quote: the Council has continued to use investment balances to temporarily fund the capital programme. This has delivered a saving on borrowing costs.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 TM AUDIT COMMITTEE
findings.headline: Council is under-borrowed relative to liability benchmark and acknowledges need for external borrowing in 2026/27
findings.detail: The liability benchmark calculation shows external debt is below the optimal level. Council explicitly acknowledges this under-borrowed position indicates future external borrowing will be required this year to align with the benchmark.
findings.matters: Under-borrowed position confirms financing gap that must be closed; affects the timing and cost of capital programme execution.

findings.quote: external debt is below the benchmark and shows that we are in an under-borrowed position in 2026/27, indicating that we will need to take some external borrowing this year.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 TM AUDIT COMMITTEE
findings.headline: No borrowing taken in Q1 2026/27 as PWLB rates remain above budget at 5.71%
findings.detail: Council has taken zero new borrowing to date in 2026/27. Treasury is actively monitoring rates and deliberately holding off borrowing to avoid taking long-term loans at current elevated PWLB rates of 5.71%. Borrowing timing will depend on cash flow requirements for the capital programme.
findings.matters: Deferral of borrowing creates timing risk for capital programme financing; higher rates when borrowing does occur will increase long-term debt service costs.
findings.figures: PWLB borrowing rates 5.71% at 30 June 2026
findings.quote: Due to the current high long-term borrowing rates there has been no borrowing taken in the year to date. The timing of any further borrowing will depend on cash flow requirements to support the Capital Programme, pending the tracking of borrowing rates.

findings.detail: Gross investment income projected at £1.539m against budget of £2.450m. The variance of £0.739m is specifically attributed to the council's strategy of delaying borrowing, which has kept investment balances lower than estimated. This directly reduces revenue-side cash generation.
findings.matters: Lower cash generation from investments constrains available liquidity; signals council is intentionally running down cash balances while waiting for better borrowing rates.
findings.figures: £1.539m projected vs £2.450m budgeted; £0.739m variance
findings.quote: The £0.739m variance to budget is due to the strategy of delaying borrowing meaning investment balances are lower than estimated.

findings.detail: Adult Social Care shows £0 variance to its £102.9m budget, but the paper explicitly names continuing "demand-led pressures associated with care packages, including transitions from Children's Services." These are being absorbed within budget now but are described as ongoing structural issues.
findings.matters: Persistent demand pressures in adult social care that are managed in-year but not resolved signal future vulnerability. If these pressures are growing year-on-year, future budgets will face tighter margins and less room to absorb shocks elsewhere.
